title: Mobility Health Observatory
text:
Welcome to the Mobility Health Observatory (MHO). This platform provides data-driven insights into how human movement, transport systems, and synthetic exposure metrics intersect with public health, road safety, and long-term population trends.

Synthetic Exposure: Integrating synthetic exposure variables to estimate population-level risk baselines across temporal and geographic boundaries.
Long-Term Dynamics: Using Age-Period-Cohort (APC) models and Lexis framework projections to isolate structural demographic changes from short-term policy shifts.

title: Spatial Risk & Exposure
text:
Evaluating spatial casualty patterns down to the Lower Layer Super Output Area (LSOA) level is essential for targeted local interventions. However, raw collision maps are notoriously misleading.
Mapping raw casualty counts by LSOA often highlights where populations live or aggregate, rather than where the underlying environment is genuinely dangerous. Furthermore, analyzing multi-decade spatial trends introduces severe geographical friction:

Boundary Drift: UK administrative boundaries are a moving target. LSOAs changed significantly between the 2011 and 2021 censuses—some merged, others split, and many had their borders adjusted.
Residence vs. Incident Multiplicity: Mapping casualties by home location reveals residential vulnerability and community risk profiles, but requires careful handling to avoid conflating residential density with localized road danger.
The Exposure Vacuum: Without a reliable measure of local movement or population at risk (exposure), a high-casualty LSOA might simply be a high-volume corridor, masking its true rate of risk.

title: Spatial Risk & Exposure
text:
Our Analytical Approach
We build micro-area spatial models that normalise casualty occurrences against synthetic exposure metrics while maintaining deterministic spatial integrity across census boundary shifts.


Show code
library(tibble)
library(tidygraph)
library(ggraph)
nodes <- tibble(id = 1:4, name = c(
    "Raw Casualty Data & Spatial Geographies\n(STATS19 & OS Boundaries)",
    "Boundary & Code Reconciliation\n• 2011 vs 2021 LSOA boundary lookups\n• Local Authority unitarisations",
    "Synthetic Exposure Modeling\n• Micro-area travel volumes\n• Population & modal baselines",
    "True Spatial Risk Surfaces\n(LSOA-level normalized exposure)"),
  node_type = c("source", "branch", "branch", "sink"), x = c(0, -3.2, 3.2, 0), y = c(2, 1, 1, 0))
edges <- tibble(from = c(1, 1, 2, 3), to   = c(2, 3, 4, 4))
graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edges, directed = TRUE)
p <- ggraph(graph, layout = "manual", x = x, y = y) +
  geom_edge_link(arrow = arrow(length = unit(5, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    end_cap = circle(28, "mm"), color = "#ced4da", width = 1.2) +
  geom_node_label(aes(label = name, fill = node_type), color = "#212529",
    fontface = "bold", label.padding = unit(14, "pt"), label.r = unit(8, "pt"), size = 4) +

  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-6.2, 6.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, 2.5)) +

title: Spatial Risk & Exposure
text:
Featured Analytical Modules

1. Residential Casualty Mapping (LSOA Home Locations)
Mapping casualties by their home LSOA shifts the focus from where collisions happen to who is being affected. This residential perspective is crucial for public health, equity, and targeted community interventions:

Vulnerability Mapping: Identifies residential neighbourhoods where inhabitants suffer disproportionate casualty rates regardless of where the crash occurred.
Socioeconomic & Demographic Context: Links residential casualty profiles directly to local deprivation indices, age structure, and household transport access.
Targeted Health Interventions: Provides local authorities with the precise spatial evidence needed to deploy community-level road safety education and active travel support.




2. Synthetic Exposure & Boundary Harmonisation
Raw counts only tell you where; spatial risk modelling tells you how dangerous.
To measure true risk, we combine casualty home locations with synthetic exposure baselines while accounting for administrative changes:

Harmonising Census Boundaries: We map historical 2011 LSOA records and post-2023 2021 LSOA census codes into a single, unified spatial frame. This ensures 10-plus year trendlines reflect actual changes on the ground rather than administrative boundary adjustments.
Synthetic Exposure Rates: By synthesising local trip generation, census commute patterns, and modal splits, we convert raw casualty counts into risk rates per unit of population exposure.
Spatial Smoothing & Noise Reduction: Micro-area data can be noisy. We apply empirical Bayes spatial smoothing to prevent small-sample LSOAs from distorting local risk maps.

title: Spatial Risk & Exposure
text:
Built on Deterministic Spatial Infrastructure
High-resolution spatial analysis requires absolute pipeline discipline to prevent silent geographic errors:






NoteSpatial Pipeline Assurance




Containerised PostGIS Engine: All spatial joins, point-in-polygon queries, and distance calculations execute within isolated Docker containers to guarantee bit-for-bit spatial reproducibility across machines.
Version-Controlled Crosswalks: Boundary conversion tables (2011-to-2021 LSOA mapping) are version-controlled alongside application code. If a boundary definition updates, the impact is tracked deterministically.
Automated Spatial Snapshots: Our automated testing suite verifies total spatial coverage and boundary completeness on every build, ensuring no unmapped LSOAs or orphan records quietly drop off the map.

title: Benchmarking & Policy Trends
text:
Local authorities, transport executive bodies, and national policymakers face a recurring problem: raw numbers rarely tell the whole story.
When a local authority reports a 15% drop in casualties over five years, is that the result of effective road safety engineering? Or is it simply driven by a shrinking young demographic, changes in regional traffic volumes, or silent shifts in administrative boundaries?
Conversely, when an authority appears to underperform, are they genuinely lagging, or are they operating under severe structural constraints, lower funding, and higher exposure?
Without controlling for external drivers, standard league tables and simple time-series dashboards reward lucky authorities and penalize those facing tough structural realities.

title: Benchmarking & Policy Trends
text:
Featured Analytical Modules

1. Age-Period-Cohort (APC) & Lexis Modeling
Traditional trend analysis lumps all annual changes into a single timeline. APC analysis disentangles three distinct drivers operating simultaneously:

Age Effects: How casualty risks vary naturally across a person’s lifespan (e.g., young driver risk vs. elderly pedestrian vulnerability).
Period Effects: External shocks affecting everyone in a specific calendar year (e.g., national speed limit changes, COVID-19 lockdowns, major weather events).
Cohort Effects: Long-term generational shifts that move with specific birth years (e.g., lower car ownership rates among younger generations, changes in safety culture).







NoteWhy This Matters for Policy



By isolating these three dimensions, we prevent misattributing a generational decline in driving (a Cohort effect) to a local road safety campaign (a Period effect). Decision-makers can evaluate whether a policy actually changed behavior or if broader societal trends did the heavy lifting.





2. Pareto Boundary & Efficiency Analysis
Evaluating local authority performance across a single metric creates perverse incentives. A council might achieve zero casualty growth by severely curtailing travel infrastructure investment, or vice versa.
Our Pareto Boundary Analysis evaluates local authorities across multiple competing dimensions simultaneously—such as safety outcomes, infrastructure expenditure, and population density:

Identifying the Optimal Frontier: We mathematically plot the “Pareto frontier”—the benchmark curve of local authorities achieving the highest possible safety outcomes for their given resource and environmental constraints.
Fair Peer Comparison: Rather than comparing a dense urban borough to a sprawling rural county, authorities are benchmarked strictly against peer councils operating on similar structural frontiers.
Target Setting: Uncovers which specific operational levers an underperforming authority must adjust to move closer to the efficient frontier.

title: Benchmarking & Policy Trends
text:
Built on Deterministic Data Integrity
Like all modules in our analytics engine, our benchmarking pipelines are engineered for complete auditability and long-term reproducibility:

Version-Controlled Boundary Adjustments: Historical trends seamlessly map LSOA 2011 to 2021 census boundary shifts without dropping records or breaking spatial joins.
Automated Regression Testing: Every model run is snapshot-tested against stored baselines to ensure upstream data revisions are caught and accounted for immediately.
Reproducible Pipeline Orchestration: Heavy demographic matrix processing is fully deterministic, allowing any historical benchmark calculation to be re-run and verified on demand.

title: Data Integrity & our Spatial Analytics Engine
text:
Building a basic dashboard is easy. Building an auditable, trustable data engine that survives changing real-world boundaries, shifting government datasets, and strict scrutiny is hard.
If your decision-making relies on long-term spatial trends—such as road safety metrics, local authority planning, or demographic shifts—you cannot afford “silent data errors.” Traditional ad-hoc dashboards often mask boundary changes or retroactive data updates, leaving you vulnerable to flawed conclusions, embarrassing discrepancies, or failed audits.
We build production-grade, highly rigorous analytics pipelines designed around four core promises:

Complete Historical Auditability (“Data Time Travel”): Government data sources and administrative boundaries change constantly. If a metric from a report published two years ago doesn’t match today’s numbers, we can instantly roll our system back to the exact data state on the day that report was generated. You never have to guess whether a shift was caused by a change in our calculations or an official update from the data provider.
Guaranteed Accuracy via National Calibration: We don’t just write queries and hope they work. Every spatial and statistical pipeline we build is continuously benchmarked and validated directly against official published national statistics (such as Reported Road Casualties Great Britain). If our baselines match the official national aggregates, you can have 100% confidence in our custom spatial breakdowns and local filtering.
Automated Data Quality & Smoke Testing: When local authorities split, boundary codes update (like LSOA shifts between census years), or incoming files contain corrupted formatting, our system catches it instantly. Instead of letting bad data silently drop rows or distort your trendlines, our automated safety checks flag issues internally before anything reaches your executive dashboard.
Zero Vendor Lock-In & Portability: Everything we build is containerised and version-controlled. You are not buying a fragile desktop spreadsheet or a proprietary black box; you are investing in a durable, open-source asset that your team can run, audit, or migrate to any cloud environment at any time.


Technical Architecture & Engineering Standards
For technical stakeholders, auditors, and engineering teams, our pipeline implements modern DataOps principles to ensure complete reproducibility, regression testing, and deterministic deployments.

library(tibble)
library(tidygraph)
library(ggraph)

nodes <- tibble(
  id = 1:5,
  name = c(
    "Source Data & Boundary Maps\n(External Feeds & OS Geographies)",
    "Data & Schema Version Control\n Data artifact versioning (DVC)\n Deterministic schema migrations (Sqitch)",
    "Isolated Spatial Database (Docker)\n Containerised spatial engine\n Automated schema & lookup validation",
    "Orchestration & Dependency DAG\n Granular dependency tracking (targets)\n Incremental build processing",
    "Automated QA & Regression Suite\n Snapshot testing on outputs (snapshotr)\n Automated calibration vs. benchmarks"
  ),
  node_type = c("source", "branch", "branch", "branch", "sink"),
  x = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  y = c(8, 6, 4, 2, 0)
)

edges <- tibble(
  from = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  to   = c(2, 3, 4, 5)
)

graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edges, directed = TRUE)

p <- ggraph(graph, layout = "manual", x = x, y = y) +
  geom_edge_link(
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(4, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    end_cap = circle(14, "mm"),
    color = "#ced4da",
    width = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_node_label(
    aes(label = name, fill = node_type),
    color = "#212529",
    fontface = "bold",
    label.padding = unit(2, "pt"),
    label.r = unit(8, "pt"),
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "source" = "#e2d9f3",
    "branch" = "#f8f9fa",
    "sink"   = "#6f42c1"
  )) +

  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",

Key Technical Components

Data Artifact & Schema Versioning: Raw datasets, boundary lookups, and database schemas are version-controlled alongside application code. Schema migrations are executed deterministically, enabling complete forward/backward rollbacks to any historical state.
Containerised Spatial Infrastructure: The underlying spatial database runs inside isolated container environments. This guarantees identical execution environments across local development, continuous integration (CI) runners, and production deployment.
Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Pipeline Orchestration: Pipeline stages—from raw data ingestion to geographic re-projection and boundary crosswalk joins—are managed via strict dependency tracking. Only modified steps are re-executed upon data or code changes, eliminating computational waste.
Automated Regression & Snapshot Testing: Analytical outputs undergo continuous automated testing against stored baseline snapshots. Any unexpected drift in aggregated row counts, spatial coverage, or indicator totals triggers build failures prior to deployment.
Calibrated Baseline Validation: Integration test suites run automated verification queries against published national aggregates. This guarantees mathematical alignment between sub-national spatial queries and top-level official control totals.

title: Data Linkage & Validation
text:
Public sector planning and spatial analytics often rely on administrative datasets as if they were objective ground truths. In practice, administrative data is complex, evolving, and prone to systemic gaps:

Scope & Definition Divergence: Police collision statistics (STATS19) capture reported crashes on public highways. Medical mortality records (ONS/Coroner ICD-10 transport codes V01–V99) record underlying cause of death regardless of location or reporting body.
Coroner Inquest Lags: Death registrations involving coroners often take months or years to resolve. Temporary holding codes (e.g., ICD-10 U50.9) delay final cause-of-death coding, creating historical discrepancies against real-time police stats.
Format & Schema Shifts: External data providers quietly update past reporting years, alter file structures, or revise reporting criteria after publication.

If an analytics system blindly ingests these datasets without cross-validation, decision-makers risk building long-term transport policies on incomplete or silently corrupted numbers.

title: Data Linkage & Validation
text:
Featured Analytical Modules

1. Cross-Source Casualty Linkage (STATS19 vs. Coroner ICD-10)
By linking police-reported collisions with medical death registrations, we reconcile structural gaps between transport reporting and medical mortality data:

Scope Reconciliation: Disentangles collisions occurring on private land, medical events preceding a crash (e.g., cardiac arrest prior to collision), and suicide classifications (X82) that may be miscategorised in initial reporting.
Coroner Lag Adjustment: Tracks historical revision curves as coroner inquests conclude, ensuring long-term mortality trendlines accurately reflect true year-of-death statistics rather than reporting lag.
Completeness Assessment: Measures under-reporting rates across transport modes and geographical regions by comparing health system admissions against police scene reports.




2. National Benchmark Calibration (RRCGB Alignment)
Custom spatial queries and sub-national filters should never exist in isolation. Every analytical output in our system is calibrated against official national standards:

Cryptographic-Level Baseline Verification: Our automated test suites run continuous verification queries comparing our pipeline outputs directly against published tables in Reported Road Casualties Great Britain (RRCGB).
Zero Discrepancy Guarantee: Matching national published totals down to the exact decimal gives stakeholders absolute confidence that custom LSOA spatial filters, local authority aggregations, and sub-population splits are mathematically sound.

title: Data Linkage & Validation
text:
Built on Open, Deterministic DataOps
Data validation is only as good as the infrastructure supporting it. Our validation pipeline treats data updates as continuous code integrations:






NoteThe DataOps Guarantee




Data Time Travel (DVC): Raw source files and intermediate datasets are version-controlled using Data Version Control. If a government dataset is quietly updated two years after initial release, we can roll the database back to any exact historical state to explain why numbers changed.
Automated Smoke Alarms (snapshotr): Regression tests flag unexpected shifts in row counts, spatial coverage, or indicator totals the second a dataset is updated—preventing bad data from quietly reaching production dashboards.
Deterministic Schema Migrations: All database schema changes and spatial lookup updates are versioned and executed programmatically, leaving a complete audit trail for external reviewers.

title: About the Mobility Health Observatory
text: The Mobility Health Observatory (MHO) is an independent data and analytics platform designed to examine the complex intersections between how we travel, our exposure to transport systems, and long-term population health across Great Britain.

title: About the Mobility Health Observatory
text:
Our Philosophy: The Denominator Problem
Traditional transport dashboards and safety reports focus overwhelmingly on outcome variables—such as raw crash counts, casualty numbers, or localized collision hotspots. While necessary, these metrics carry a fundamental limitation: they map where events happen, not where risk actually resides. High crash counts in a specific area often simply reflect high traffic volumes or dense populations.
To truly understand transport safety and environmental health, we must shift our focus to the denominator: exposure.
By leveraging advanced statistical modeling, small area estimation (SAE), and high-resolution government surveys, MHO builds robust synthetic exposure variables. This allows us to calculate true population-level risk baselines across temporal, spatial, and demographic boundaries.

title: About the Mobility Health Observatory
text:
Core Methodological Pillars
MHO synthesizes nearly three decades of peer-reviewed academic research into modern, reproducible open-source infrastructure. Our analytical work centers on three key areas:

Synthetic Exposure Modeling: Overcoming the limitations of sparse physical traffic counters and travel surveys by combining rich national datasets (such as the Census and National Travel Survey) with small area estimation techniques to model local-level mobility patterns.
Age-Period-Cohort (APC) Dynamics: Utilizing sophisticated demographic modeling to disentangle the overlapping effects of aging populations, macroeconomic/policy periods, and generational cohort shifts on long-term safety and health trends.
Multi-Outcome Health Integration: Moving beyond single-issue crash analysis to evaluate the broader systemic trade-offs of urban mobility—including active travel health benefits, air quality exposure, and environmental stressors.

title: About the Mobility Health Observatory
text:
Research Heritage & Rigor
The insights hosted on this platform build upon decades of academic inquiry and peer-reviewed methodology in transport safety, spatial statistics, and applied epidemiology. By moving this research out of static academic papers and into an interactive, open-access observatory, MHO aims to support researchers, policymakers, and public health advocates with transparent, reproducible data tools.


Open Science & Reproducibility
In alignment with modern scientific best practices, MHO is built on a fully decoupled, reproducible architecture: * Modularity: Heavy analytical models and small area estimations are run in isolated version-controlled repositories. * Traceability: Data artifacts and analytical outputs are tracked and versioned using Data Version Control (DVC). * Open Source: The entire observatory website is built using Quarto, with code and methodologies shared openly for peer review and replication.
